title: Proof
body_md:
Write $P=(-\Delta)^{\frac{n}{2}}$, $f=(n-1)!|x|^{n\gamma}e^{nu}$ and $T=Pu-f$, so that $\operatorname{supp}T\subset\{0\}$. For $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$, we have $\int_{\mathbb R^n}P\phi\,\mathrm d y=0$ and $(1+\log(1+|y|))P\phi\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$; in odd dimensions the latter follows from \cite[Proposition~2.1]{Hyder2019}.
Therefore, a scaling and the dominated convergence theorem give
\begin{equation*}
 \left\langle T,\phi(\cdot/\varepsilon)\right\rangle
 =\int_{\mathbb R^n}[u(\varepsilon y)-u(0)]P\phi(y)\,\mathrm d y-\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\phi(x/\varepsilon)\,\mathrm d x\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation*}
By the structure theorem for distributions supported at a point (se \cite[Theorem~6.24(d) $\And$ Theorem~6.25]{Rudin1991}), this forces $T=0$. 

Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:NormalSolutionHMM} to this global solution gives $u=v+p$, where $v$ has logarithmic growth and $p$ is a polynomial. The growth assumption on $u$ implies that $p$ is constant, so $u$ is normal.

label: lem:radial-kernel-g
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Beta identity \eqref{eq:beta-gamma} gives
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{\Gamma(1+i\xi/2)}{\Gamma(n/2+i\xi/2)}
 =\frac{1}{\Gamma(n/2-1)}
 \int_0^1 r^{i\xi/2}(1-r)^{n/2-2}\,\mathrm d r.
\end{equation*}
With $r=e^{-2s}$, this becomes
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{\Gamma(1+i\xi/2)}{\Gamma(n/2+i\xi/2)}
 =\frac{2}{\Gamma(n/2-1)}\int_0^\infty e^{-i\xi s}f_n(s)\,\mathrm d s
 =\frac{2}{\Gamma(n/2-1)}\widehat f_n(\xi).
\end{equation*}
Using \eqref{eq:g-hat} and $\widehat{\widetilde f_n}=\overline{\widehat f_n}$ proves \eqref{eq:g-autocorrelation-revised} with $d_n=\frac{2^{4-n}}{\Gamma(n/2-1)^2}$. Evenness and positivity follow immediately.
	
For $t>0$, using $\widetilde f_n(s)=f_n(-s)$ and changing variables $s\mapsto-s$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{gn convol}
 g_n(t) =d_n\int_\mathbb R f_n(t-s)f_n(-s)\,\mathrm d s=d_n\int_0^\infty f_n(t+s)f_n(s)\,\mathrm d s,
\end{equation}
For $t\ge1$ and $s>0$, $f_n(t+s)\le Ce^{-2t}e^{-2s}$. Since $f_n\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, this gives $g_n(t)\le Ce^{-2t}$. The corresponding bound for $t\le-1$ follows by evenness.
	
The integral identity \eqref{int gn} follows from
	\begin{equation*}
		\int_\mathbb R g_n(t)\,\mathrm d t=\widehat g_n(0)=\frac{1}{\beta_n}.
	\end{equation*}
    
	Now we prove that $g_n'(t)<0$ for $t>0$.
For $n>4$, direct differentiation gives
	\begin{equation*}
	\frac{\,\mathrm d^2}{\,\mathrm d s^2}\log f_n(s)
	=-\frac{4(\frac{n}{2}-2)e^{-2s}}{(1-e^{-2s})^2}<0\text{ for }s>0.
	\end{equation*}
	Set $K(x,y)=f_n(x-y)$ and fix $x_1<x_2$ and $y_1<y_2$.
If $y_2\ge x_1$, then $K(x_1,y_2)=0$, so
\[
 \det[K(x_i,y_j)]_{i,j=1}^2
 =K(x_1,y_1)K(x_2,y_2)\ge0.
\]
If $y_2<x_1$, all four arguments are positive. Since
$(\log f_n)'$ is strictly decreasing and $x-y_2<x-y_1$,
integration over $x\in[x_1,x_2]$ gives
\[
 \log\frac{f_n(x_2-y_2)}{f_n(x_1-y_2)}
 >
 \log\frac{f_n(x_2-y_1)}{f_n(x_1-y_1)}.
\]
Exponentiating and rearranging yields
\[
 \det[K(x_i,y_j)]_{i,j=1}^2
 =f_n(x_1-y_1)f_n(x_2-y_2)
  -f_n(x_1-y_2)f_n(x_2-y_1)>0.
\]
By \eqref{eq:g-autocorrelation-revised}, we get $g_n(x-y)=d_n\int_\mathbb R K(x,z)K(y,z)\,\mathrm d z$.
Expanding the product of the two determinants and applying
Fubini's theorem and the symmetry, we get

\[
 \det[g_n(x_i-y_j)]_{i,j=1}^2
 =d_n^2\iint_{z_1<z_2}
 \det[K(x_i,z_j)]_{i,j=1}^2
 \det[K(y_i,z_j)]_{i,j=1}^2
 \,\mathrm d z_1\,\mathrm d z_2>0.
\]
The strict inequality follows because both determinants are
nonnegative on $z_1<z_2$ and strictly positive on the set
$z_1<z_2<\min\{x_1,y_1\}$, which has positive measure.
The integrand is nonnegative everywhere and strictly positive
when $z_1<z_2<\min\{x_1,y_1\}$.
Since $f_n(0)=0$ for $n>4$, differentiation of
\eqref{gn convol} and integration by parts give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
g_n'(t)=d_n\int_0^\infty f_n'(s+t)f_n(s)\,\mathrm d s=-d_n\int_0^\infty f_n(s+t)f_n'(s)\,\mathrm d s.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Averaging these expressions yields
\[
 g_n'(t)=\frac{d_n}{2}\int_0^\infty
 f_n(s+t)f_n(s)
 \left[
 \frac{f_n'(s+t)}{f_n(s+t)}
 -\frac{f_n'(s)}{f_n(s)}
 \right]\,\mathrm d s<0,
 \qquad t>0,
\]
because the preceding derivative formula shows that $f_n'/f_n$ is strictly decreasing.
 
For $n=4$, a direct computation gives $\hat{g}_4(\xi)=\frac{1}{\xi^2+4}$ and  $g_4(t)=\frac14e^{-2|t|}$. 
  
For $n=3$,  differentiating \eqref{gn convol} under the integral sign gives
   \begin{equation*}
   	g_3'(t)=d_3\int_0^\infty f_3'(s+t)f_3(s)\,\mathrm d s<0,
   	\qquad t>0.
   \end{equation*}
This proves the strict decrease of $g_n$ on $(0,\infty)$.
   
   By \eqref{eq:g-hat}, $\widehat g_3(\xi)\sim |\xi|^{-1}$ as $|\xi|\to\infty$. Then the Fourier inversion gives the logarithmic singularity of $g_3$ at the origin. The same multiplier formula shows that $g_3$ is smooth on $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$.

label: def:TP2
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:TP2}
A kernel $K:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is called \emph{strictly totally positive of order two} if
\[
 \det\begin{pmatrix}
 K(t_1,s_1)&K(t_1,s_2)\\
 K(t_2,s_1)&K(t_2,s_2)
 \end{pmatrix}>0
\]
whenever $t_1<t_2$ and $s_1<s_2$.

title: Proof
body_md: Taking Fourier transforms gives $a_{n,0}\widehat h=0$.  Since $a_{n,0}$ is nonzero away from the origin, we get $\operatorname{supp}\widehat h\subset\{0\}$. By \cite[Theorem~6.24(d) $\And$ Theorem~6.25]{Rudin1991}, we get $\widehat h=\sum_{|k|\leq N}c_k\delta^{(k)}_0$. Since $\operatorname{supp}\widehat h\subset\{0\}$ and $b_n(0)>0$, the equation $\xi^2b_n\widehat h=0$ implies $\xi^2\widehat h=0$. By \cite[Theorem~3.1.16, p.~67]{HormanderI}, $\xi\widehat h=c\delta_0$ for some constant $c$. By the fact that $\xi\delta_0'=-\delta_0$, a second application of the same theorem gives $\widehat h=a\delta_0'+b\delta_0$ for some constants $a$ and $b$. Taking the inverse Fourier transform completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is similar to the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:radial-kernel-g}. From the Beta identity \eqref{eq:beta-gamma} and a change of variables, we can write
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{\Gamma((k+i\xi)/2)}{\Gamma((k+n+i\xi)/2)}
 =\frac2{\Gamma(n/2)}\int_0^\infty
 e^{-(k+i\xi)s}(1-e^{-2s})^{n/2-1}\,\mathrm d s.
\end{equation*}
Recall that the Fourier symbol of $A_{n,k}$ is $a_{n,k}(\xi)$, given in \eqref{eq:mode-symbol}. Then, by letting
\begin{equation*}
 h_{n,k}(s)=e^{-ks}(1-e^{-2s})^{n/2-1}\mathbf1_{(0,\infty)}(s),
\end{equation*}
we have
\begin{equation*}
 G_{n,k}=\frac{2^{2-n}}{\Gamma(n/2)^2}h_{n,k}*\widetilde h_{n,k},
\end{equation*}
which is exactly \eqref{eq:G-beta}. Euler's formula \eqref{eq:hyp-euler} then gives \eqref{eq:G-hyper} and \eqref{eq:G-diagonal} follows by evaluating at $t=0$.


The convolution representation gives evenness and strict positivity.
Moreover,
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d^2}{\,\mathrm d s^2}\log h_{n,k}(s)
 =-\frac{4(\frac n2-1)e^{-2s}}{(1-e^{-2s})^2}<0,
 \qquad s>0.
\]
Since $h_{n,k}>0$ on $(0,\infty)$ and vanishes on
$(-\infty,0]$, the determinant argument in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:radial-kernel-g} applies with $h_{n,k}$ in
place of $f_n$ and gives \eqref{eq:G-positive-minors}.
For $0\le s<t$, taking
$(t_1,t_2)=(s,t)$ and $(s_1,s_2)=(0,s+t)$ in that inequality
and using evenness gives $G_{n,k}(s)^2-G_{n,k}(t)^2>0$. Since $G_{n,k}>0$, this proves strict decrease on $(0,\infty)$.

label: thm:mu2
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:mu2-odd-sector}, $\mu_2(\alpha,k)$ is the principal eigenvalue in the class of odd functions.  Let $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ be the corresponding odd eigenfunction, normalized by $\|f\|_2=1$ and chosen positive on $(0,\infty)$. Define the odd function $h=W_\alpha^{\frac{1}{2}}f$. Then, since $W_\alpha$ decays exponentially, we have $h\in L^1\cap L^2$, $\widehat h(0)=0$ and $\widehat h(\xi)=O(\xi)$ as $\xi\to0$. Since $\widehat h(\xi)=O(\xi)$ and $a_{n,0}(\xi)\sim\beta_n\xi^2$ as $\xi\to0$, the quotient $|\widehat h(\xi)|^2/a_{n,0}(\xi)$ is bounded near zero. Away from zero, $a_{n,0}^{-1}$ is bounded and $\widehat h\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ by Plancherel's theorem. Thus the radial inverse quadratic form is finite:
\[
 \frac1{2\pi}\int_\mathbb R
 \frac{|\widehat h(\xi)|^2}{a_{n,0}(\xi)}\,\mathrm d\xi<\infty.
\]

We claim that for every $n\ge3$, every integer $k\ge1$ and every $\xi\in\mathbb R$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:symbol-order}
	a_{n,k}(\xi)>a_{n,0}(\xi).
\end{equation}
Indeed, by definition \eqref{eq:mode-symbol}, we have the recurrence relations
\begin{align}
	\frac{a_{n,k+2}(\xi)}{a_{n,k}(\xi)}
	&=\frac{\xi^2+(n+k)^2}{\xi^2+k^2}>1,
	\label{eq:k-recurrence}\\
	a_{n+2,k}(\xi)
	&=\bigl(\xi^2+(n+k)^2\bigr)a_{n,k}(\xi).
	\label{eq:n-recurrence}
\end{align}
For even dimensions, we begin with $a_{2,k}(\xi)=\xi^2+k^2>a_{2,0}(\xi)=\xi^2$. Then the inequality follows from \eqref{eq:n-recurrence}.

For odd dimensions, start with $n=3$.  With $s=\frac{|\xi|}{2}$, the reflection identities for the gamma function give
\begin{equation*}
a_{3,0}(\xi)=8s\left(s^2+\frac14\right)\tanh(\pi s),
\qquad a_{3,1}(\xi)=8s(s^2+1)\coth(\pi s).
\end{equation*}
Thus $a_{3,1}>a_{3,0}$.  Formula \eqref{eq:k-recurrence} gives $a_{3,k}>a_{3,0}$ for every even $k\ge2$ and it gives $a_{3,k}>a_{3,1}>a_{3,0}$ for every odd $k\ge3$. Finally, \eqref{eq:n-recurrence} propagates the inequality to all odd dimensions.




Set $f_+(t)=\sqrt2\,f(t)$ for $t>0$.
Since $f$ is odd and $\|f\|_{L^2(\mathbb R)}=1$, we have
$\|f_+\|_{L^2(0,\infty)}=1$.
By Plancherel's identity, \eqref{odd spec rad 1}, and \eqref{eq:symbol-order},
\begin{align*}
 \mu_2(\alpha,k)
 &=\frac1{2\pi}\int_\mathbb R
   \frac{|\widehat h(\xi)|^2}{a_{n,k}(\xi)}\,\mathrm d\xi\\
 &<\frac1{2\pi}\int_\mathbb R
   \frac{|\widehat h(\xi)|^2}{a_{n,0}(\xi)}\,\mathrm d\xi\\
 &=\left\langle
   f_+,\mathscr K_{\alpha,0}^{\mathrm o}f_+
   \right\rangle_{L^2(0,\infty)}\\
 &\le r(\mathscr K_{\alpha,0}^{\mathrm o})
       \|f_+\|_{L^2(0,\infty)}^2=1.
\end{align*}
By the Birman--Schwinger principle,
\begin{equation*}
     \operatorname{ind}^{-}(L_{\alpha,k})=\#\{j:\mu_j(\alpha,k)>1\},
\end{equation*}
where $\operatorname{ind}^{-}$ denotes the number of negative eigenvalues and both sides count multiplicities. Since $\mu_2(\alpha,k)<1$, this number is at most one. If zero is an eigenvalue of $L_{\alpha,k}$, then \eqref{equiv L K} gives $\mu_1(\alpha,k)=1$. Thus $L_{\alpha,k}$ has no negative eigenvalues, and zero is its principal eigenvalue and is simple.

It remains to prove the monotonicity of $\psi_{\alpha,k}$. Since $\psi_{\alpha,k}\in H^n(\mathbb R)$ and $W_\alpha,W_\alpha'\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)$, we can differentiate the equation \eqref{eq:generalized-eigenpair} with respect to $t$. Then, the odd function
\begin{equation*}
 z_{\alpha,k}:=-W_\alpha^{1/2}\partial_t\psi_{\alpha,k}\in L^2(\mathbb R)   
\end{equation*}
 satisfies
\begin{align}
\bigl(\mu_1(\alpha,k)I-\mathscr K_{\alpha,k}^{\mathrm o}\bigr)z_{\alpha,k}&=-W_\alpha^{1/2}A_{n,k}^{-1}
\bigl(W_\alpha'\psi_{\alpha,k}\bigr)\nonumber\\
&=- W_\alpha(t)^{1/2}\int_0^\infty
 \bigl[G_{n,k}(|t-s|)-G_{n,k}(t+s)\bigr]W_\alpha'(s)\psi_{\alpha,k}(s)\,\mathrm d s\nonumber\\
 &=:F_{\alpha,k} \text{ on } (0,\infty).\nonumber
\end{align}
Here in the second equation, we use oddness and the half-line kernel \eqref{eq:odd-angular-kernel}. Since $ W_\alpha'(t)=n\,\partial_t v_\alpha(t)\,W_\alpha(t)<0$ for $t>0$ and $G_{n,k}$ is strictly decreasing, $F_{\alpha,k}(t)>0$ for every $t>0$.

By \eqref{eq:mu2-odd-sector} and the positivity and self-adjointness of the operator,
\[
 \left\lVert \mathscr K_{\alpha,k}^{\mathrm o}\right\rVert_{L^2\to L^2}
 =\mu_2(\alpha,k)<\mu_1(\alpha,k).
\]
Consequently, we can invert the operator $(\mu_1(\alpha,k)I-\mathscr K_{\alpha,k}^{\mathrm o}\bigr)$ to obtain
\begin{equation*}
 z_{\alpha,k}=\frac{1}{\mu_1(\alpha,k)}\sum_{j=0}^\infty
 \left(\frac{\mathscr K_{\alpha,k}^{\mathrm o}}{\mu_1(\alpha,k)}\right)^j F_{\alpha,k},   
\end{equation*}
with convergence in $L^2(0,\infty)$. The kernel \eqref{eq:odd-angular-kernel} is positive, so $z_{\alpha,k}\ge \frac{F_{\alpha,k}}{\mu_1(\alpha,k)}>0$ almost everywhere. Since $z_{\alpha,k}$ and $F_{\alpha,k}$ are continuous, this inequality holds everywhere on $(0,\infty)$. Therefore, we conclude that
\begin{equation*}
    \partial_t\psi_{\alpha,k}(t)=-\frac{z_{\alpha,k}(t)}{W_\alpha(t)^{1/2}}<0
 \text{  for }t>0.
\end{equation*}

label: eq:M-halfline
title: Proof
body_md:
We extend $M$ to an odd function on $\mathbb R$. By definition $M'=W_\alpha q_\alpha$. Applying $B_n^{-1}$ to \eqref{eq:q-jacobi} and integrating once, we obtain $-q_\alpha'=g_n*M$. In other words, we can write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:M-halfline}
 -\left(\frac{M'}{W_\alpha}\right)'(t)
 =\int_0^\infty\bigl[g_n(|t-s|)-g_n(t+s)\bigr]M(s)\,\mathrm d s.
\end{equation}
The kernel $g_n(|t-s|)-g_n(t+s)$ is strictly positive because $g_n$ is strictly decreasing. 

On the other hand, since $\frac{W_\alpha'}{W_\alpha}=nv_\alpha'$, \eqref{eq:strict-concavity} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:N-halfline}
 -\left(\frac{W_\alpha'}{W_\alpha}\right)'(t)
 =\int_0^\infty\bigl[g_n(|t-s|)+g_n(t+s)\bigr]W_\alpha(s)\,\mathrm d s.
\end{equation}

Differentiating the mass identity \eqref{eq:W-mass} gives
\begin{equation*}
 \lim_{t\to\infty}M(t)=\frac{1}{2}\int_\mathbb R W_\alpha q_\alpha\,\mathrm d t=\beta_n>0.
\end{equation*}
Let $R=\frac{M}{W_\alpha}$. Then $R(0)=0$ and $R(t)\to+\infty$ as $t\to\infty$. Multiplying \eqref{eq:M-halfline} by $W_\alpha$, multiplying \eqref{eq:N-halfline} by $M$ and subtracting gives
\begin{align}\label{eq:ratio-identity}
 -\left({W_\alpha}R'\right)'(t)
 ={}&W_\alpha(t)\int_0^\infty
 \bigl[g_n(|t-s|)-g_n(t+s)\bigr]W_\alpha(s)[R(s)-R(t)]\,\mathrm d s\notag\\
 &-2M(t)\int_0^\infty g_n(t+s)W_\alpha(s)\,\mathrm d s.
\end{align}


Now we prove that $R\geq 0$.
If $R$ were negative somewhere, then it would have a negative global minimum at some $t_0>0$.  At $t=t_0$, the left side of \eqref{eq:ratio-identity} is nonpositive.  At $t=t_0$, the first term on the right is nonnegative, while the second is strictly positive because $M(t_0)<0$.  This is impossible.  Thus $R\ge0$.


Now we prove that $R>0$.
If $R(t_0)=0$ for some $t_0\in (0,\infty)$, then $t_0$ would be a global minimum equal to zero. The second term of the right hand side of \eqref{eq:ratio-identity} would vanish, but the first would be strictly positive because $R$ is not identically zero.  This is again impossible.  Hence $R>0$ and $M=RW_\alpha>0$ in $(0,\infty)$.

For $n=3$, $g_3$ has a logarithmic singularity at zero but
belongs to $L^1(\mathbb R)$, so its convolutions with the bounded
functions $M$ and $W_\alpha$ are continuous.
The identities therefore hold pointwise and the same minimum argument applies.
